nacelle.e: PIE word *néh₂us Borrowed from French nacelle (“rowing boat, skiff; gondola (of a hot-air balloon, etc.).

nadir.e: From Medieval Latin nadir, from Arabic نَظِير السَّمْت (naẓīr as-samt), composed of نَظِير (naẓīr, “counterpart, corresponding to”) and السَّمْت (as-samt, “the zenith”).
nadir.x: The nadir of the sun is the axis of the shadow projected by the Earth.

naiad.e: From Latin Nāïas, from Ancient Greek Νᾱϊάς (Nāïás, “naiad”), from νάω (náō, “to flow”).
naiad.x: A Naiad loved him, and forbade him to hold intercourse with any other woman under pain of loss of sight.

nakedness.e: From Middle English nakednesse, from Old English nacodnes (“nakedness”); equivalent to naked + -ness. Cognate with West Frisian neakenens (“nakedness”).

namaste.e: Learned borrowing from Sanskrit नमस्ते (namaste, literally “a bow to you”).

nameless.e: From Middle English nameles, equivalent to name + -less. Cognate with Dutch naamloos (“nameless”), German namenlos (“nameless”), Danish navnløs (“nameless”), Swedish…
nameless.x: Environmental DNA analysis suggests that the number of species of bacteria that remain nameless to date may well be on the order of many thousands.

namely.e: From Middle English namely, nameliche, namelike, equivalent to name + -ly.
namely.x: Some of the students — namely Paul, Alice and Jake — seem to have trouble with geometry.

namesake.e: Mid-17th century. Equivalent to name + sake. From the phrase “for (one's) name's sake”, first found in Bible translations as a rendering of a Calque of Hebrew לְמַעַן…
namesake.x: The statesman Winston Churchill has a namesake, the American novelist Winston Churchill.

nanosecond.x: I just know that the nanosecond I take my eyes off my phone, somebody's going to steal it.

nanotechnology.e: From nano- + technology. Popularized in 1986 by Eric Drexler.

napalm.x: When leaked, the controversial documents proved to be political napalm.

naphtha.x: The Common Room and the Library were lit by anbaric light, but the Scholars preferred the older, softer naphtha lamps in the Retiring Room.

napkin.e: From Middle English napekyn, napkyn, equivalent to nape (“cloth”) + -kin (diminutive suffix).

narcissism.e: From obsolete German Narzissismus (now Narzissmus by haplology), from Narziss (“Narcissus”) + -ism.

narcissist.e: From Narcissus (“a character in Greek mythology who became obsessed with his own reflection”) + -ist.

narcissus.e: Borrowed from Latin narcissus, from Ancient Greek νάρκισσος (nárkissos), ultimately either from Pre-Greek or related to νάρκη (nárkē).

narcolepsy.e: From French narcolepsie. By surface analysis, narco- + -lepsy, from Ancient Greek ναρκόω (narkóō, “put to sleep”) + λῆψις (lêpsis, “seizure”).
narcolepsy.x: Excitement-induced narcolepsy caused him to sleep through the most important events of his life.

narcotic.e: From Middle English narcotyk, from Middle French narcotique (from Old French narcotique, noun use of adjective) and directly from Medieval Latin narcōticum, from Ancient…
narcotic.x: "Real San Juan Colorado," he said. "Excitable people like you are the better for narcotics. Heavens! don't bite it! Cut - and cut with reverence!"

narrate.e: In English (recorded only since 1656, but until the 19th century stigmatized as 'Scottish') apparently from narration.
narrate.x: The documentary will narrate the rise and fall of the historic club.

narration.e: From Middle French narration, from Old French narracion, from Latin narrātiō. By surface analysis, Latin narr- + -ate + -ion.
narration.x: The film used voice-over narration to explain the story.

narrative.e: Borrowed from Middle Scots narrative, nerrative, from Middle French narratif, from Latin narrātīvus, from narrō (“to narrate”).
narrative.x: But wise through time, and narrative with age.

narrowly.e: From Middle English narowly, equivalent to narrow + -ly.
narrowly.x: They regarded the new idea rather narrowly.

narrowness.e: From Middle English narwenesse; equivalent to narrow + -ness.

nasal.e: From Middle English, from Medieval Latin nāsālis, from nāsus (“the nose”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix). Doublet of nasalis.
nasal.x: "Are you sure you're OK?" she said with a nasal Australian accent.

nascent.e: Borrowed from Latin nāscēns, nāscentis, present participle of nāscor (“to be born”). Doublet of naissant.
nascent.x: Marks of the makers : the initials of the maker and the arms of the town : a lion nascent with three flames.

nationalisation.e: From French nationalisation. By surface analysis, nationalise + -ation.

nationalism.e: Borrowed from French nationalisme, equivalent to national + -ism.

nationality.e: From national + -ity, perhaps after French nationalité; ultimately from Latin nātio (“nation, people”).
nationality.x: By living in the country for five years, you are entitled to get nationality.

nationalize.e: From French nationaliser. By surface analysis, national + -ize.
nationalize.x: The government plans to nationalize the energy industry.

nationwide.x: There was a nationwide search on for the bankrobbers.

naturalist.e: From natural + -ist. Piecewise doublet of naturalista.

nausea.e: From Middle English nausea, a borrowing from Latin nausea, from Ancient Greek ναυσία (nausía, “sea-sickness”), from ναῦς (naûs, “ship”), from Proto-Indo-European…
nausea.x: He got nausea after two hours of travelling on the plane.

nauseous.e: From Latin nauseōsus (“causing nausea”), corresponding synchronically to nausea + -ous.
nauseous.x: And then what proper person can be partial / To all those nauseous epigrams of Martial?

nautical.x: I was mostly unfamiliar with the nautical terms used in the sailing documentary.

nautilus.e: From Latin nautilus, from Ancient Greek ναυτίλος (nautílos, “paper nautilus, sailor”).
nautilus.x: Living species of the externally shelled nautiluses do not possess an ink sac.

naval.e: From Middle English naval, from Middle French naval, from Latin nāvālis; equivalent to navy + -al.

navel.x: Sweeter than the muſk of Tatar, the morning breeze from the navel of every flower raviſhed perfume.

navigable.e: From Middle French navigable, from Latin navigabilis.
navigable.x: This Web site isn't very navigable. I can't tell which image links to which page.

navigate.e: First attested in 1588; borrowed from Latin nāvigātus, the perfect passive participle of nāvigō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from nāvis (“ship”) + -igō, from…
navigate.x: He navigated the bomber to the Ruhr.

navigation.e: Borrowed from Middle French navigation, from Latin nāvigātiōnem, accusative singular of nāvigātiō (“sailing, navigation”), from nāvigō (“sail”).

navigator.e: From Latin nāvigātor. By surface analysis, navigate + -or.
navigator.x: He felt having a Micronesian navigator meant he needed a pureblooded Polynesian, preferably a Hawaiian, as captain.

neaten.x: She made a frantic attempt to neaten her hair.

nebulous.e: Inherited from Middle English nebulous, from Middle French nebuleus, from Latin nebulōsus (“full of mist, foggy, cloudy”), from nebula (“mist, vapour, cloud”), from…

necessitate.e: From earlier necessitat, from Medieval Latin necessitātus, perfect past participle of necessitō (“to make necessary”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix, of participial…
necessitate.x: The early departure of her plane necessitated her waking up at 4 a.m.

necessity.e: From Middle English necessite, from Old French necessite, from Latin necessitās (“unavoidableness, compulsion, exigency, necessity”), from necesse (“unavoidable…
necessity.x: I bought a new table out of necessity. My old one was ruined.

neckerchief.e: From Middle English nekkyrchefe, neckercheve, equivalent to neck + kerchief.
neckerchief.x: The Boy Scout wore a red neckerchief, the ends clasped with a sliding knot ornament.

necktie.x: Oh I have been to Ludlow fair / And left my necktie God knows where / And carried half way home, or near, / Pints and quarts of Ludlow beer.

necromancer.e: An alteration of nigromancer after necromancy, equivalent to necromancy + -er.

necromancy.e: Circa 1300, from Middle English nigromancye, from Old French nigromancie, from Medieval Latin nigromantia, from Latin necromantia, from Ancient Greek νεκρομαντεία…
necromancy.x: And in one word for all, Nagomancy, or Necromancy; by inspecting, consulting, and divining by, with, or from the dead.

necrophilia.e: From necro- (Ancient Greek νεκρός (nekrós, “corpse, dead”)) + -philia (Ancient Greek φιλία (philía, “affection”)), after German Nekrophilie (in Krafft-Ebing 1887).
necrophilia.x: A woman in Sweden has been accused of necrophilia after investigators found some 100 skeleton parts in her apartment.

necropolis.e: Borrowed from Koine Greek νεκρόπολις (nekrópolis, “city of the dead, cemetery”) (used to describe part of the city of Alexandria, Egypt), from Ancient Greek νεκρός…
necropolis.x: You think London isn't a necropolis? Let me tell you it is. And people love it. Our cemeteries are popular tourist attractions.

necrosis.e: From Ancient Greek νέκρωσις (nékrōsis), equivalent to necro- + -osis.
necrosis.x: Usually gangrene will follow necrosis unless the dead tissue is resected.

nectar.e: From Latin nectar, from Ancient Greek νέκταρ (néktar, “nourishment of the gods”), from Proto-Indo-European *neḱ- (“perish, disappear”) + *-tr̥h₂ (“overcoming”), from…
nectar.x: They pourd in soveraine balme and Nectar good, / Good both for erthly med'cine and for hevenly food.

needless.e: From Middle English needlees, nedelees, nedeles, equivalent to need + -less.
needless.x: This new project of yours will only be a needless expense.

nefarious.e: From Latin nefārius (“execrable, abominable”), from nefās (“something contrary to divine law, an impious deed, sin, crime”), from ne- (“not”) + fās (“the dictates of…
nefarious.x: Aliens have a nefarious connotation in many science fiction books.

negate.e: From Latin negātus, perfect passive participle of negō (“to deny, refuse, decline”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).
negate.x: The investigation tending to negate any supernatural influences.

negation.e: From Middle English negacioun, from Old French negacion, from Latin negātiō (“a denial; negative word”). Morphologically negate + -ion.
negation.x: But it pleased her to play on my passion / And whet me to pleadings / That won from her mirthful negations / And scornings undue.

negligence.e: From Middle English necligence, negligence, from Old French negligence, from Latin neglegentia.
negligence.x: The Woodwalton signalman, Rose, who was severely censured in Captain Tyler's report, behaved with great negligence.

negligent.e: From Middle English necligent, negligent, from Old French negligent, from Latin negligēns.
negligent.x: The driver was found negligent in causing the accident.

negotiate.e: c. 1598; borrowed from Latin negōtiātus, perfect active participle of negōtior (“to do business, trade”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from negotium (“business”) +…
negotiate.x: We negotiated the contract to everyone's satisfaction.

negotiation.e: Borrowed from Middle French négociation, or from Latin negotiatio (“the carrying on of business, a wholesale business”), from negotiari (“to carry on business”).
negotiation.x: The specifics of the contract are still under negotiation.

negotiator.e: Borrowed from Latin negōtiātor (“merchant, banker”), equivalent to negotiate + -or.

negroni.e: Borrowed from Italian negroni, from surname Italian Negroni, from Italian negri (“black”) + Italian -oni (“(ablative) from, of”).
negroni.x: A curly-haired 20-something sat down across the bar from us, opened a book, and ordered a bowl of olives and a negroni.

negus.e: Named after Colonel Francis Negus (1670–1732), its creator.
negus.x: ‘I could sure use a cup of negus and maybe some hot soup,’ he sniffs.

neigh.e: Inherited from Middle English neyen, from Old English hnǣġan, from Proto-West Germanic *hnaijan, from Proto-Germanic *hnajjaną (“to neigh”).

neighbour.e: From Middle English neighebour, neighbour, neyghebour, from Old English nēahġebūr (“neighbour”), from Proto-West Germanic *nāhwagabūrō, from Proto-Germanic *nēhwagabūrô…
neighbour.x: They′re our neighbours across the street.

nematode.e: Borrowed from translingual Nematoda, from Ancient Greek νηματώδης (nēmatṓdēs, “fibrous, in filaments”), from νῆμα (nêma, “thread, yarn”) + -ώδης (-ṓdēs, “-like”).
nematode.x: Nematodes are free-living, soil-dwelling microscopic worms.

neophyte.e: Borrowed from Latin neophytus, from Ancient Greek νεόφυτος (neóphutos, “newly planted”), from νέος (néos, “new”) + φυτόν (phutón, “plant, child”).
neophyte.x: In this scene Lupita, the neophyte, is counselled by more weathered professionals about the rules and regulations of whoring.

nepotism.e: Borrowed from French népotisme, from Italian nepotismo, from Latin nepōs (“nephew”), a reference to the practice of popes appointing relatives (most often nephews) as…
nepotism.x: Nepotism can get you very far in the world if you've got the right connections.

nervously.x: He paced nervously as he waited for the important phone call.

nestle.e: From Middle English nestlen, from Old English nistlan, nestlian, nistlian (“to make or build a nest”), from Proto-West Germanic *nistilōn (“to build or occupy a nest.

nestling.e: From Middle English nestling, equivalent to nest + -ling.

nether.x: The disappointed child’s nether lip quivered.

nettle.e: From Middle English netle, netel, from Old English netle, netele, netel, from Proto-West Germanic *natilā (cognate with Old Saxon netila, Middle Dutch netele (modern…

neural.e: From Ancient Greek νεῦρον (neûron, “a sinew, nerve”) + -al.

neuralgia.e: From New Latin neuralgia, from Ancient Greek νεῦρον (neûron, “nerve”) + ἄλγος (álgos, “pain”). By surface analysis, neur- + -algia.
neuralgia.x: A century later, the UK’s post-Brexit dispute with Brussels about Northern Ireland’s trading arrangements with the EU has stirred the same neuralgia.

neurasthenia.e: From neur- + asthenia, after Italian nevrastenia. By surface analysis, neur- (“nerve”) + a- (“not”) + sthen- (“strength”) + -ia (“disease”).

neuron.e: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek νεῦρον (neûron, “nerve”), doublet of nerve and sinew. By surface analysis, neuro- + -on.

neuropathy.x: Long-standing diabetes often causes neuropathy in the retinas, fingertips, and toes.

neurosurgeon.x: With considerable difficulty, Blake Taylor, the neurosurgeon who operated on her, stopped the bleeding.

neurotoxin.x: There were stretches of days when the lakes were closed because of the algae. It sometimes secreted neurotoxins that could be fatal.

neurotransmitter.x: Anyway, my neurotransmitters are scrambled and they're going to stay scrambled. But I can do okay as long as other people don't know about me.

neutral.e: From Middle French neutral (compare modern French neutre), from Latin neutrālis. By surface analysis, neuter + -al.
neutral.x: I am neutral regarding the issue of gay marriage.

neutrality.e: From Middle French neutralité, from Medieval Latin neutralitas. Morphologically neutral + -ity.
neutrality.x: Men who possess a state of neutrality in times of public danger, desert the interest of their fellow subjects.

neutralize.e: From French neutraliser (first attested in 1642). By surface analysis, neutral + -ize.

neutrino.e: Coined by Italian physicist Enrico Fermi in 1933 from neutron + the Italian diminutive suffix -ino; by surface analysis, neutr(o)- + -ino.

neutron.e: From neutral + -on; by surface analysis, neutr(o)- + -on. Coined by Scottish-Australian physicist William Sutherland in 1899 in a paper in the Philosophical Magazine.

neverland.e: From Never + land. The term was most famously used in J.M. Barrie's Book, Peter Pan, as the name of the fictional island that the Darling children visit with the title…

nevertheless.e: From Middle English nevertheles, never-þe-les, nevere-þe-lesse. By surface analysis, never (“not at all”) + the + less; compare never the wiser.
nevertheless.x: He saw a monstrosity of a dog trodding on the sidewalk, unleashed, with a haughty man besides it; nevertheless, he continued his treacherous plight.

newcomer.e: From Middle English newe-comere, equivalent to new- + comer. Compare Old English nīwcumen (“new comer, neophyte, novice”).

newly.e: From Middle English newly, newely, neweliche, from Old English nīewlīċe (“newly”), equivalent to new + -ly.
newly.x: She smelled the newly budding flowers.

newness.x: The newness of the car meant it still had that funny smell.

newsagent.x: The papers are freely available in Sydney bookshops and newsagents.

newscaster.x: Take Linda, a thirty-nine-year-old newscaster who relished her career but began to hear the alarm ringing on her biological clock.

newspeak.e: From Newspeak, coined by George Orwell in 1949. Equivalent to new + speak.

newton.e: Named after the English scientist Sir Isaac Newton (1642–1726) in 1948.
newton.x: For quotations using this term, see Citations:newton.

nibble.e: The verb is derived from Late Middle English nebillen, nebyll (“to peck away at (something), nibble; (figurative) to attempt to sing (a part of a song)”).
nibble.x: Giant parrots nibbled seed from the children's fingertips and my sister peeled a couple of satsumas for the lemurs.

niche.e: Unadapted borrowing from French niche, from Middle French niche, from Old French niche, from nicher (“to make a nest”) (modern French nicher), from Vulgar Latin…
niche.x: I managed to carve out a niche for myself in the world of investigative journalism.

nickel.x: That is just objectively terrifying regardless of contexts! He looks like if a nickel did cocaine!

nickname.e: From Middle English neke name, alteration (due to a rebracketing of an ekename as a nekename) of earlier ekename (“nickname”), from eke (“additional”) + name.
nickname.x: "The Big Apple" is a common nickname for New York City.

nicotine.x: The nicotine in tobacco has been held to produce anaphrodisiac effects, in spite of such literary commendation as J.M. Barrie's My Lady Nicotine.

nigella.e: Borrowed from translingual Nigella, from Late Latin nigella. Doublet of nielle.

nightcap.x: Winston wore a nightcap to stave off the cold.

nightgown.e: From Middle English nyght gowne. By surface analysis, night + gown.

nightingale.e: Inherited from Middle English nyghtyngale, nightingale, niȝtingale, alteration (with intrusive n) of nyghtgale, nightegale, from Old English nihtegala, nihtegale…
nightingale.x: Some admired the external beauties of the objects they beheld, like the nightingale in love with the roſe.

nightlife.x: Rio de Janeiro boasts the best nightlife in South America.

nightlight.x: They made you give up / your nightlight / and your teddy / and your thumb.

nightmarish.x: Meanwhile, the everyday landscape becomes more nightmarish and unmanageable each year.

nightshade.e: From Middle English nyȝtschade, niȝteschode, nyght shade, from Old English nihtsċada, from Proto-West Germanic *nahtskadō (“nightshade”), corresponding to night + shade.

nightstand.e: From night (“the conventional time for a person to be in bed”) + stand (“an object which supports things”).
nightstand.x: He always kept a full glass of water on the nightstand.

nighttime.e: From Middle English nyght tyme, nyȝttyme, equivalent to night + time. Compare Dutch nachttijd, German Nachtzeit, Danish nattetid, Swedish nattetid.

nihilism.e: Probably borrowed from French nihilisme, German Nihilismus, or Late Latin nihilismus.
nihilism.x: Although Lexiteers have little patience for the national nihilism of “Davos Man,” the globalist elite, we are no xenophobes.

nihilistic.x: The bombing comes over a week after ISD released a report about how nihilistic worldviews are fueling violence in the US and Europe.

nimbus.e: Learned borrowing from Latin nimbus (“dark cloud”). Doublet of nimb.

ninth.e: From Middle English nynthe, nynte, from Old English niġoþa, from Proto-Germanic *newundô; the -n- was reinserted by analogy with nine.

nipple.e: From earlier neple, nypil, neble, believed to be a diminutive of nib, neb (“tip, point”), equivalent to nib + -le.

nirvana.e: Borrowed from Sanskrit निर्वाण (nirvāṇa, “blown or put out, extinguished”), from निस् (nis, “out”) + वा (vā, “to blow”), the second part cognate with Russian ве́тер…

nitpick.e: From nit + pick, originally referring to literally removing tiny louse eggs by hand.
nitpick.x: Someone will invariably nitpick about any spelling error posted to the forums.

nitrate.x: The pinkness of bacon – or cooked ham, or salami – is a sign that it has been treated with chemicals, more specifically with nitrates and nitrites.

nitrogen.x: By molar fraction, nitric oxide contains equal parts nitrogen and oxygen.

nobility.e: From Old French nobilité, from Latin nobilitas. Equivalent to noble + -ity.
nobility.x: The castle was once home to the Scottish nobility.

nocturne.e: Borrowed from French nocturne (literally “nocturnal”), from Latin nocturnus. Doublet of notturno.

noiseless.x: The movements of the cat were noiseless as it approached the mousehole.

noisy.x: This market is the noisiest and swarmiest centre of noisy and swarming Florence, and I always like to pass through it on that account.

nomad.e: From Middle French nomade, from Latin Nomas (“wandering shepherd”), from Ancient Greek νομάς (nomás, “roaming, wandering, esp.
nomad.x: The life of the people called the Nomads or Grazyers...

nomadic.e: From Ancient Greek νομαδικός (nomadikós), equivalent to nomad (“a member of a society or class of herdsmen”) + -ic (forming adjectives).

nomenclature.e: Borrowed from Latin nōmenclātūra (“a calling by name, list of names”), from nōmen (“name”) + calāre (“call”). Doublet of nomenklatura.

nominal.x: He gave me only a nominal sum for my services.

nomination.e: From Middle English nominacion, nomination, from Middle French nominacion and its etymon Latin nōminātiō, from the verb nōminō (“to name; to nominate”).
nomination.x: Her nomination for the award came as a pleasant surprise.

nonchalant.e: Borrowed from French nonchalant, from Old French nonchaloir (“to be unconcerned”), from non- (“not”) + chaloir (“to have concern for”), from Latin non (“not”) + calēre…
nonchalant.x: We handled the whole frenetic situation with a nonchalant attitude.

nonentity.x: Imagine them not even getting his name right, Weasley, it's almost as though he's a complete nonentity, isn't it?

nonetheless.e: A modification of natheless after none, from Middle English natheles, from Old English nān þȳ lǣs, nā þē lǣs, nā þȳ lǣs. Univerbation of none + the + less.
nonetheless.x: That's proof to Freire that the party has room for moderate Republicans who are nonetheless loyal Republicans.

nonexistence.x: The nonexistence of Father Christmas and the Tooth Fairy came as something of a shock.

nonexistent.x: His social skills are nonexistent: he chewed with his mouth open all through dinner.

nonfiction.x: Encyclopedias, how-to manuals and biographies are all considered nonfiction and so are kept in the nonfiction section.

nonplussed.e: From nonplus (“state of bewilderment or perplexity”, noun) or nonplus (“to bewilder or perplex (someone)”, verb) + -ed (suffix forming adjectives, and the past tense and…
nonplussed.x: I could not discern what she meant, and I would not ask her: I was nonplussed.

nonstop.x: There's a nonstop flight to Mauritius, but I'm not sitting on the same plane for thirteen hours.

nonviolence.x: From this theological perspective, the spectrum of violences has to give way to a spectrum of nonviolences.

noodle.e: Borrowed from Dutch noedel (“noodle”), or from its etymon German Nudel (“piece of pasta, noodle”).
noodle.x: She slurped a long noodle up out of her soup.

noose.e: From Middle English nose (“noose, loop”), of unclear origin. Possibly from Old French nos or Old Occitan nous, nos, nominative singular or accusative plural of nou…

normalcy.x: When so I ponder, here apart, / What shallow boons suffice my heart, / What dust-bound trivia capture me, / I marvel at my normalcy.

normality.e: From normal + -ity, perhaps modelled on French normalité.
normality.x: Jessie was going to wear pants to school, but her brother persuaded her to wear shorts to preserve normality.

normalize.x: We'll need to normalize these statements before we can compare them.

northeast.e: From Middle English northest, from Old English norþēast, equivalent to north + east.
northeast.x: Chungshe is one of eleven villages in Liuchia township, Tainan county (see Maps 2 and 3). It lies about 30 kilometers northeast of Tainan city.

northeastern.e: From Middle English norþesterne, from Old English norþēasterne, equivalent to north + eastern.

northwest.e: From Middle English northwest, from Old English norþwest, equivalent to north + west.

nosegay.x: Tacked to Miss Trixie's desk was a large sign that said miss trixie with an old-fashioned nosegay drawn in crayon in one corner.

nostalgia.x: Seeing food at camp similar to his mother's cooking sent a wave of nostalgia through him.

nostril.e: From Middle English nostrille, from Old English nosþyrel. Compare Old Frisian nosterle (“nostril”), modern West Frisian noaster (“nostrill”).

notable.e: Inherited from Middle English notable (“worthy of note, profitable, useful”), in some senses from Anglo-Norman notable (“noteworthy”), from Latin notābilis (“noteworthy…

notary.e: From Middle English notarie, from Old French notarie (French notaire), from Latin notārius.

notation.e: From Latin notātiō, equivalent to notate + -ion or note + -ation.
notation.x: This section lists all algebraic notation used in this book.

notch.e: Recorded since 1577, probably a rebracketing of an otch, from Middle French oche (“notch”), itself from the Old French verb ochier (“to notch”), of uncertain origin, but…

noticeable.x: The dismissal of a player who left Arsenal for Manchester City before joining Tottenham gave the home players and fans a noticeable lift.

notification.e: From Middle French notification, from Old French notificacion, from Latin nōtificātiō.

notify.e: From Middle English notifien, a borrowing from Old French notifier, notefiier.

notion.e: From Latin nōtiō (“a becoming acquainted, a taking cognizance, an examination, an investigation, a conception, idea, notion”), from nōscō (“to know”).
notion.x: What hath been generally agreed on, I content myself to assume under the notion of principles.

notorious.e: From Late Middle English notoryous, from Medieval Latin nōtōrius (“evident, known; famous, well-known; infamous”), from Latin nōtus (“known, recognized.
notorious.x: You notorious ſtinkardly bearevvard, do's my breath ſmell?

nougat.e: From French nougat, from Occitan nogat, from noga (“nut”), ultimately from Latin nux (“nut”) + -atus (“-ate, forming adjectives and substantives having or resembling some…
nougat.x: When you make a nougat of large dimensions, put in the almonds a few at a time.

nourish.e: From Middle English norischen, from Old French nouriss-, stem of one of the conjugated forms of norrir, from Latin nutriō (“to suckle, feed, foster, nourish, cherish…
nourish.x: He planteth an ash, and the rain doth nourish it.

nourishment.e: From Middle English norisshement, from Middle French, from Old French norissement, from norrir, equivalent to nourish + -ment.
nourishment.x: Many ultraraces do not include much nourishment from organizers.

novella.e: Borrowed from Italian novella. Doublet of novel.

novelty.e: From Middle English novelte, from Old French novelté (Modern French nouveauté), from the adjective novel, ultimately from Latin novellus.
novelty.x: Reconciling profound enquiry with clearness, and truth with novelty.

novena.e: From Ecclesiastical Latin novēna, from Latin novēnus (“nine [each]”).

novice.e: From Middle English novice, novys, from Anglo-Norman novice, Middle French novice, itself borrowed from Latin novīcius, later novitius (“new, newly arrived”) (in Late…
novice.x: I'm only a novice at coding, so my programs frequently have bugs that more experienced programmers would avoid.

noxious.e: From Latin noxius (“hurtful, injurious”), from noxa (“hurt, injury”), from nocere (“to hurt, injure”); see nocent.

nozzle.e: From Middle English noselle, equivalent to nose + -le (diminutive suffix).
nozzle.x: At length the acme of a typical Mexican scene was reached when the burros unceremoniously raised their nozzles and brayed loud and long.

nucleus.x: This collection will form the nucleus of a new library.

nudge.e: Circa 17th century, perhaps of North Germanic origin, related to Norwegian nugge, nyggje (“to push, rub, shove”), Icelandic nugga (“to rub, massage”), from the root of…
nudge.x: Since the machine was showing two lemons and a cherry, I decided to try a nudge.

nudity.e: From nude + -ity. Compare Late Latin nūditās.
nudity.x: In places such as Scandinavia, public nudity is legal.

nuisance.e: From Middle English noysaunce, from Anglo-Norman nusaunce, nussance and Old French nuisance, from nuisir (“to harm”), from Latin nocēre. Doublet of nocence and nocency.
nuisance.x: The neighbor's dog barking throughout the night is a right nuisance - I'm going to complain.

numbering.e: From Middle English nombrynge; equivalent to number + -ing.

numeral.e: As an adjective, from Middle English numeral, numerall, from Latin numerālis (“pertaining to a number”), from numerus (“a number”). As a noun, via Middle French numeral.
numeral.x: Compare the numeral for the product with the original decimal numeral.

numerator.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin numerātor.

numerous.e: From Middle English numerous from Latin numerōsus (“numerous, abundant; harmonious”), from numerus (“number”). Doublet of numerose. Analyzeable as numero- + -ous.
numerous.x: The reasons to refrain are numerous.

nunchaku.e: Borrowed from Okinawan 双節棍 (nunchaku) (compare Japanese 双節棍 (nunchaku)), probably from Hokkien 兩節棍 /两节棍 (nn̄g-chat-kùn, literally “two-segment cudgel”), from 兩 /两 (nn̄g…

nuncio.e: From Spanish nuncio, from Latin nūntius (“envoy”).

nunnery.e: From Middle English nonnery, nonnerie, equivalent to nun + -ery. (brothel): Compare typologically Czech nevěstinec (< nevěstka < nevěsta).
nunnery.x: Get thee to a nunnery, why wouldst thou be a breeder of sinners?

nuptial.e: Borrowed from Latin nūptiālis (“pertaining to marriage”), from nūptiae (“wedding”), from nūbō (“to marry, to take as husband”).
nuptial.x: To prevent the erosion of his own authority, Basil is persuaded to re-enact his father's crime — to unflower the servant girl on her nuptial night.

nursery.e: From Middle English noricerie, norserye (“children's nursery; state of being fostered or nursed.

nurture.e: From Middle English norture, noriture, from Old French norriture, norreture, from Late Latin nutritura (“nourishment”), from Latin nutrire (“to nourish”).

nutmeg.e: From Middle English notemege, notemuge, a partial translation of Medieval Latin nux muga, a variant of Medieval Latin nux muscata (“musky nut”).

nutrient.e: Borrowed from Latin nūtriēns, present participle of nūtriō (“to suckle, nourish, foster”).

nutrition.e: Borrowed from Middle French nutrition, from Old French nutricion, from Latin nutritio.
nutrition.x: Proper nutrition – and even more important, proper hydration – is crucial in preventing and recovering from both fevers and colds.

nutritious.e: Learned borrowing from Latin nūtrītius, from nūtrītus, from nūtrīre.

nutshell.e: From Middle English notschelle, from Old English hnutsċiell, from Proto-West Germanic *hnutskallju, equivalent to nut + shell.

nylon.e: Coined by the company DuPont in 1938. According to the company, the name was formed from the random generic syllable nyl- + the common fiber suffix -on (as in rayon and…
nylon.x: I tore a hole in my nylons while walking home through the woods.

nymphomania.e: Borrowed from New Latin, from Latin nympha + -mania. By surface analysis, nympho- + mania.
nymphomania.x: Camphor, however, has been used to counteract the conditions arising from nymphomania.
